szoveg_eredeti:
“In any truly advanced civilization that gets depicted [in science fiction], you really see two pillars of scientific progress. One is some form of AGI, and the other a simulation. And I was always more drawn to the idea of simulation.” – Joon Sung Park, Co-Founder and CEO of Simile

Before Joon Sung Park and I had ever met, he simulated the conversation. What questions would Mario, or a person like Mario, ask him? What would I find most interesting to dig into? I do not know how closely I adhered to my facsimile, though I wish I did.

Joon has an advantage in rehearsing these encounters, and thousands of others. He is the Co-founder and CEO of Simile, an applied AI company building a foundation model of human behavior. That involves creating digital twins of real people – like a writer or podcaster – and simulating how they might react to certain circumstances. As you might imagine, that’s an attractive proposition for many companies: CVS Health, for instance, can test a new pricing policy against thousands of simulated patients. A bank can model how customers will react before announcing a fee change. Joon’s ambitions stretch far beyond these cases, though, and Simile has raised more than $300 million, most recently at a $2 billion valuation, to pursue them.

The portrait artist always paints themselves. I loved this line from Joon, who happens to be a gifted painter in his own right. When apprehending a piece of art – whatever the medium – I can sometimes forget to consider what it tells us about the author rather than the subject.

“Emotional rigor.” Another phrase of Joon’s that I’ve been sitting with. This was how he described the intensity one needs to build to paint a beautiful painting of someone. You need to build this deep, rigorous connection. This is a universal lesson, I think, and especially true in writing.

Contradictory superpowers. Another really sharp heuristic (can you tell I enjoyed this conversation quite a lot?). When it comes to hiring, this is what Joon looks for: someone with two strengths that rarely go together. For example, a colleague with deep scientific seriousness and a very playful side.

Working backwards. Joon’s ultimate goal is not to give Simile a question and have it make a prediction. It is to give a “wicked” problem like climate change and have it simulate a superabundance of possible paths to help us find the best one.

Who wins when everything is predictable? If simulation becomes as ubiquitous as Simile suggests it might, how do companies compete with one another? Is “strategy,” as a broad discipline, solved? Joon pointed to a few thoughts on where edge might still live – namely in point of view, proprietary data, and compute. Now, this is just a thought experiment, of course. But two of those three presumably redound to the world’s best-resourced companies, which is far from ideal.

When I asked Joon what book he'd assign to everyone, he named The Catcher in the Rye, which he first read at around 14 or 15. He was careful to say that the books that matter most are deeply personal, but Holden Caulfield's visceral portrait of a young mind stuck with him. Earlier in our conversation, he also pointed to Asimov's Foundation series as a core inspiration for Simile, and particularly the idea of psychohistory: giving a simulator a desired end state and working backwards to find the path there.

What I’m reading, watching, and into this week:

Jon Ronson has a new book out, The Castle. I’m only a few pages in, but given that I’ve loved all of his other bizarre, freewheeling investigations, I suspect I’ll like it quite a bit.

Grok Bot is really very good at this point. I suspect this form factor – persistent, proactive, task-specific bots overseen by an orchestrator – will become the default for professional work. It’s the closest thing to having a collection of digital coworkers.

Mario Gabriele: If you can predict the future, then you could be the world’s greatest hedge fund ever.

Joon Sung Park: So it’s a really interesting question. Simile is an applied AI layer that basically allows you to predict people’s behavior at the level of individuals and populations. We can predict people’s behavior with 85% plus accuracy.

Mario Gabriele: And the ultimate goal is to simulate all 8 billion humans and predict the future in some sense?

Joon Sung Park: Yes, it is about representing people in our society and also try to understand the interaction between them. A lot of the companies that we work with, they want to talk to their niche population all the time, but they can maybe, if they’re lucky, to get to talk to them once, but we create simulations of them once, then they can ask them any questions.

So this is actually the strength for a simulation. So the problems that we want to go after is really ask questions like, well, how to solve climate change? Can we actually find out the signals for democracy that’s about to collapse? So this is what social scientists would call wicked problems. I often, before interviews, simulate how the interview might go.

What are some of the interesting questions that you might ask me today?

Mario Gabriele: A pharmacy chain wants to know why its patients stop taking their pills. A bank is about to change what it charges. A CEO is preparing to walk into an earnings call. None of them know what will happen. But Joon Sung Park just might. Joon is the co-founder and CEO of Simile. In 2023, as a Stanford PhD student, he published a paper that put 25 AI agents in a small virtual town and watched them throw a Valentine’s party.

Simile is that idea grown up: digital twins of real people, built from hours of interviews that let companies like CVS test a decision on thousands of simulated customers before making a real one. That pitch has helped Simile raise more than $300 million and reach a $2 billion valuation. In this episode, we discuss Joon’s past as a painter, why the end market for a simulation company might be a hedge fund, and what happens to strategy once everyone can see the future.
